summary: GeoNexus finds the places on Earth that look most like any spot on the Moon or Mars, then lets you drive a rover on both and compare them side by side. You click a site on a 3D globe built from NASA LOLA and MOLA elevation data. A two-stage model then searches 1.4 million Earth terrain cells: a self-supervised terrain encoder retrieves likely matches, and landform measurements made on identical 16 km patches on every world re-rank them by shape: ridges, pits, roughness and crater-like relief. Each Earth twin comes with a confidence badge, a percentile and the evidence behind it. Our Discovery Atlas ran 252 Mars and Moon sites and found 871 Earth candidate areas, 802 of them outside the 36 published analog sites we checked against. Testing rovers and training crews on Earth is far cheaper than on Mars, and GeoNexus helps teams find, explain and compare those test sites in minutes.
details:
What it does

GeoNexus answers one question for any point on the Moon or Mars: where on Earth can we practise this? It has three parts.

  1. Mission console. A 3D globe of Mars or the Moon is built from NASA MOLA and LOLA elevation data with NASA Trek imagery. Click anywhere and GeoNexus names the place (IAU nomenclature), runs the model and opens the best Earth twin beside it.
  2. Earth-twin model. It works in two stages.
  • Retrieve: our S1 terrain encoder, a SimCLR model trained without labels on elevation patches, ranks 1.4 million Earth cells by terrain shape. Physical screens keep dry, barren ground, and cold deserts for polar sites.
  • Re-rank: for the top 200 candidates we cut the same 16 km × 16 km patch at 500 m per pixel on both worlds, using an azimuthal-equidistant projection that works even at the poles. We then measure anisotropy (ridges and grooves), pit density (craters), multi-scale roughness and a landform class. The final five twins are at least 500 km apart. Each one shows a confidence level, its percentile among all eligible Earth cells, and which measurements agree.
  1. Rover drive and sensors. The same rover drives on the planet and on its Earth twin at the same time, under each world's gravity, slope, atmosphere and temperature. Live charts compare elevation, slope, density and temperature and give a per-channel similarity score. Earth weather is live.

Discovery Atlas. We ran 252 Mars and Moon query sites through the model and clustered the Earth twins into 871 candidate areas. Without being told where known sites are, the model rediscovered 2 of 36 published analog sites. High-confidence matches land on a known site 8.1% of the time, against 0.4% for random eligible Earth cells (about 20 times more often). The other 802 areas are new candidates, each with its evidence and its distance to the nearest known site.

Benefits and impact

  • Mission and rover teams can shortlist Earth test sites for traverse, navigation and sampling tests in minutes, with the evidence visible.
  • Polar regions are fully supported, which matters for Artemis lunar south-pole planning.
  • The side-by-side drive makes reduced gravity and alien terrain understandable for students and the public.

How we built it

  • Front end: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui (Base UI), CesiumJS (3D globes), Chart.js, WebGL2 (landing-page Mars rendered from MOLA heights).
  • Back end and model: Python with NumPy, DuckDB, Rasterio and Pillow. PyTorch was used to train the S1 SimCLR terrain encoder.
  • Data pipeline: integrated Moon, Mars and Earth tables built from NASA PDS, USGS, NOAA, ESA/Copernicus and OpenLandMap sources.
  • Hosting: Hugging Face Spaces (app) and GitHub (code and dataset).

What makes it creative

  • Most analog lists are compiled by hand. GeoNexus searches the whole planet the same way for every query and shows its reasoning.
  • One metric patch geometry for all three worlds, so a crater on the Moon and a crater in the Sahara are measured with the same ruler, even at the poles.
  • Matching is tied to experience: you do not just read a score, you drive both places.

What we considered

  • Honesty about limits. Scores are experimental resemblance indices, not proof of analog quality or safety. Features smaller than about 1 km (for example single dunes) are below the 500 m resolution. Antarctica has no land-cover data, so polar matches use a relaxed screen, and the app labels it.
  • Data rights: every source keeps its own terms and is cited in the dataset's ATTRIBUTION.md.
  • Speed: stage-2 re-ranking adds under 2 s per query once an area is cached.
